Advocate, on behalf of Mr. D. N. Prajapati, Advocate Hon'ble Shri Justice Sanjay Kumar Jaiswal Order on Board 12.11.2024 1.

This appeal has been preferred by the Insurance Company under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, challenging the award dated 04.01.2016 passed by the Chief Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Raipur (C.G.) in Claim Case No.155/2011.
2.

entities.text: Chief Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Raipur
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
The facts necessary for disposal of the present appeal, in brief, are that on 12.03.2011, when deceased Shiv Kumar Gayakwad was returning home from village Dondekala on TVS Super Moped,
respondent No.5 Omdas Gilahre driving the offending vehicle i.e. Mazda bearing registration No.
CG 04 JB 2689 rashly and negligently dashed him between village Matiya and Dondekala, as a result of which, he suffered grievous injuries on his head and ribs and died on the spot.
The claimants who are the wife and children of the deceased preferred an application before the Tribunal claiming total compensation of Rs.66.26,000/-.

Learned Tribunal, after considering the evidence and documents brought on record, awarded total compensation of Rs.38,94,920/- with interest @
6% per annum, from the date of application till its realization, in favour of the claimants for their irreparable loss.
While passing the impugned award, the Tribunal has fastened the liability of payment of compensation upon the Insurance Company against which this appeal has been filed by the Insurance Company.
3. Learned counsel for Insurance Company submits that at the relevant point of time, the driver did not have a valid and effective driving licence.

He disputed the finding given by the Tribunal in para-12 of its award that the licence of the driver was not valid from 15.05.2013 to 11.12.2013 whereas due to technical error in the Computer, it was wrongly mentioned in the licence from 15.05.2010 to 11.12.2013.

He further submits that the driver had an LMV licence whereas he was driving the light goods vehicle (LGV), therefore, there has been a breach of policy condition and the insurance company cannot be held liable for payment of compensation.
He further submits that the Tribunal has erred in taking 50% of the income towards future prospects whereas it should have been 30% as per the age of the deceased.
Hence, prays for allowing the appeal.

4. On the other hand, it has been argued on behalf of learned counsel appearing for respondents 5 to 6 i.e. the driver and owner that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the finding of the Claims Tribunal holding the Insurance Company liable for payment of compensation is just and proper and requires no interference in the same.

5. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.

sentences.text: The first contention of the Insurance Company is that at the time of accident the driver had an LMV licence whereas he was driving a Light Goods Vehicle (LGV).

He submits that though there is an endorsement of heavy goods vehicle and heavy passenger transport vehicle in the licence Ex.D-2,
the same was valid till 14.05.2010 and thereafter it was not renewed.

The Insurance company also disputes the finding of the Tribunal given in para-12 of its award that the details of Ex.D-2 has been verified by the Assistant Regional Transport officer stating that due to technical error in the Computer, it was wrongly mentioned that the licence of the driver regarding transport vehicle was not valid from 15.05.2010 to 11.12.2013 whereas the same was not valid only from 15.05.2013 to 11.12.2013.
7.

The issue with respect to persons having a particular class of license authorizing to drive a particular type of vehicle, but on the date of accident found driving the vehicle other than the type of vehicle mentioned in the licence, but of the same category, has been considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Company Limited reported in (2017) 14 SCC 663 and held as under:-
"59.

entities.text: Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Company Limited reported in (2017) 14 SCC 663
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Section 10 of the Act requires a driver to hold a licence with respect to the class of vehicles and not with respect to the type of vehicles.
In one class of vehicles, there may be different kinds of vehicles.
If they fall in the same class of vehicles, no separate endorsement is required to drive such vehicles.
As light motor vehicle includes transport vehicle also, a holder of light motor vehicle licence can drive all the vehicles of the class including transport vehicles.
It was pre-amended position as well the post- amended position of Form 4 as amended on 28-03- 2001.

Any other interpretation would be repugnant to the definition of "light motor vehicle" in Section 2(21) and the provisions of Section 10(2)(d), Rule 8 of the Rules of 1989, other provisions and also the forms which are in tune with the provisions.

Even otherwise the forms never intended to exclude transport vehicles from the category of 'light motor vehicles' and for light motor vehicle, the validity period of such licence hold good and apply for the transport vehicle of such class also and the expression in Section 10(2)(e) of the Act 'Transport Vehicle' would include medium goods vehicle,
medium passenger motor vehicle, heavy goods vehicle, heavy passenger motor vehicle which earlier found place in Section 10(2)(e) to (h) and our conclusion is fortified by the syllabus and rules which we have discussed.

60. Thus we answer the questions which are referred to us thus:
60.1. ''Light motor vehicle'' as defined in Section 2(21) of the Act would include a transport vehicle as per the weight prescribed in Section 2(21) read with Sections 2(15) and 2(48).

Such transport vehicles are not excluded from the definition of the light motor vehicle by virtue of Amendment Act No.54 of 1994.
60.2.

A transport vehicle and omnibus, the gross vehicle weight of either of which does not exceed 7500 kg. would be a light motor vehicle and also motor car or tractor or a road roller, 'unladen weight' of which does not exceed 7500 kg.

as provided in Section 10(2)(d) is competent to drive a transport vehicle or omnibus, the gross vehicle weight of which does not exceed 7500 kg. or a motor car or tractor or road-roller, the "unladen weight" of which does not exceed 7500 kg.
That is to say, no separate endorsement on the licence is required to drive a transport vehicle of light motor vehicle class as enumerated above.
A licence issued under Section 10(2)(d) continues to be valid after Amendment Act 54/1994 and 28-03-2001 in the form.

60.3. The effect of the amendment made by virtue of Act No.54 of 1994 w.e.f. 14-11-1994 while substituting clauses (e) to (h) of Section 10(2) which contained "medium goods vehicle" in Section 10(2)
(e), "medium passenger motor vehicle" in Section 10(2)(f), "heavy goods vehicle" in Section 10(2)(g)
and "heavy passenger motor vehicle" in Section 10(2)(h), with expression "transport vehicle" as substituted in Section 10(2)(e) related only to the aforesaid substituted classes only.
It does not exclude transport vehicle, from the purview of Section 10(2)(d) and Section 2(41) of the Act i.e. light motor vehicle.
8. Undisputedly, the driver had a licence for driving Light Motor Vehicles (LMV) which was valid from 19.02.2004 to 18.02.2024.
The accident took place on 12.03.2011.
As such, at the time of accident, the driver of the vehicle in question had a valid LMV licence.
As per the provisions of Section 2(21) of MV Act, all vehicles whose weight is less than 7500 Kgs. are to be treated as 'Light Motor Vehicle'.
Perusal of the particular of registration of the offending vehicle would show that its unladen weight was 2850 Kgs and laden weight was 7450 i.e. less than 7500 Kgs.
Therefore, the offending vehicle would fall under LMV category and the driver did have a valid licence to drive Light Motor Vehicle (LMV).
Even otherwise, in the light of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Mukund Dewangan (supra), the first contention of the Insurance Company would not be sustainable.
9. The second contention of the Insurance Company is that the future prospects should have been 30% of the income instead of 50%.
At the time of accident, deceased Shiv Kumar was aged about 42 years and he was working as an Assistant Teacher in the Education Department.

Hence, in the light of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd., Vs.
Pranay Sethi and Others, (2017) 16 SCC 680, the future prospects would be 30% of the income instead of 50% as wrongly held by the Tribunal.

sentences.text: Hence, the second contention of the Insurance Company is accepted.
10. The Tribunal has held the income of deceased at Rs.2,69,280 per annum as per his salary slips.
Hence, the income of the deceased is taken as Rs.2,69,280 per annum.
After adding 30% towards future prospects i.e. Rs.80,784/-, the amount comes to Rs.3,50,064/-.

Considering the fact that there are 4 claimants who are the wife & children of the deceased, deduction towards personal expenses would be 1/4th of the income instead of 1/3rd as wrongly held by the Tribunal.

The impugned award stands modified to the extent that the claimants shall now be entitled for a total compensation of Rs.38,65,672/- instead of Rs.38,94,920/- as awarded by the Tribunal.
Rest of the conditions of the impugned award shall remain intact.
